sample_unit: FDA-cleared radiology AI devices (57 target pathology entries)

links.outcome: Expected PPV/FDR of FDA-cleared radiology AI at intended-population prevalence versus reported sensitivity and specificity
links.effect: Median sensitivity, specificity, and ROC-AUC exceeded 90%, yet FDRs were often high; a large vessel occlusion detector (90.6% sensitivity, 88.8% specificity) had PPV 29.3% and FDR 70.7% at 4.87% prevalence.
links.quote: For example, a large vessel occlusion detector with 90.6% sensitivity and 88.8% specificity was estimated to have a PPV of 29.3% and an FDR of 70.7% at a prevalence of 4.87%, meaning most positive AI alerts would be false positives.

links.outcome: Whether public 510(k) summaries report sensitivity, specificity, and test set prevalence enabling predictive value estimation
links.effect: Authors conclude 510(k) summaries should consistently report sensitivity, specificity, and test set prevalence so PPV, FDR, NPV, and FOR can be estimated locally; current accuracy metrics do not indicate expected false positives.
links.quote: Public 510(k) summaries should consistently report sensitivity, specificity, and test set prevalence so that radiologists and other stakeholders can estimate PPV, FDR, NPV, and FOR for their own patient populations before implementation.

screen.reason: Empirical analysis modeling the false-positive paradox across 38 FDA-cleared radiology AI devices using 510(k) reported metrics and real-world disease prevalences; does not test a specific deployment intervention.
